lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3, which promise did the world's countries make to children in 1989? (The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.) Today: what those rights are, and our part in them.

In 1948 the United Nations wrote down rights for every person in the world. In 1989 it agreed a special list for children: the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Nearly every country has promised to keep it.
The Convention has 54 articles, or parts. It says every child under 18 has rights, whoever they are, wherever they live, whatever language they speak and whatever they believe.

Some of the rights: to be safe from harm, to go to school and to have a name. Children have the right to health care, and to rest and play. They have a right to a say in what affects them, and to fair treatment.
Rights cannot be taken away, and no right matters more than another. Grown-ups, and the governments of countries, have a duty to protect children's rights.
Rights come with responsibilities. If I have the right to learn, I have the responsibility to let others learn too. If I have the right to be listened to, I listen to others.
A right is not the same as a want. Every child has the right to play, but not a right to the newest toy. Rights are what every child needs to be safe, healthy and to grow up well.
Try it in the world: with your friends, write a charter for your town on a sign: three rights, and the responsibility that goes with each one. Next: who runs a town?

exercises.prompt: Who has the rights in the Convention on the Rights of the Child?
exercises.hint: Remember: whoever they are, wherever they live.
choices: only children who are good at school
exercises.explain: Every child under 18, whoever and wherever they are.

exercises.prompt: In which year was the Convention on the Rights of the Child agreed?
exercises.hint: It was in grade 3's lesson too: near the end of the 1900s.
exercises.explain: The United Nations agreed it in 1989.

exercises.prompt: Every child has the right to go to school.
exercises.hint: Look at the table of rights.
exercises.explain: True: article 28 says every child has the right to learn.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a right in the Convention?
exercises.hint: A right is something every child needs to grow up well.
exercises.explain: Rest and play is a right (article 31). The others are wants.

exercises.prompt: Match each right to the responsibility that goes with it.
exercises.hint: Your right is everyone else's right too.
exercises.explain: Learn and let others learn; be heard and listen; be safe and keep others safe; play and let others play.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a right, or a want?
exercises.hint: Could a child grow up well without it?
exercises.explain: Rights: school, safety and health care. Wants: a new bike, sweets and holidays: nice, but not needed to grow up well.

exercises.prompt: Who has a duty to protect children's rights?
exercises.hint: Who has the power to keep children safe and give them schools?
exercises.explain: Grown-ups and the governments of countries have the duty to protect children's rights.

exercises.prompt: A right can be taken away as a punishment.
exercises.hint: Remember what the Convention says about rights.
exercises.explain: False: rights cannot be taken away. A child who breaks a rule still has the right to be safe, to food and to learn.

exercises.prompt: How many articles, or parts, does the Convention have?
Bram talks loudly while Zara is trying to read. Whose right is he forgetting?
exercises.hint: Every right comes with a responsibility towards others.
choices: the teacher's right to a holiday
exercises.explain: Zara has the right to learn; Bram's responsibility is to let her learn.

exercises.prompt: Why is having a name a right?
exercises.hint: Think about how a new baby is registered.
choices: a name shows you exist and belong
so that you can buy things
exercises.explain: A name (and a country) shows that a child exists and belongs, so the child can be protected and go to school.

exercises.prompt: The rights in the Convention are the same for every child, whatever language they speak or believe.
exercises.explain: True: every child has the same rights.

exercises.prompt: Tilly's class wants to make a new rule for playtime. Which right says they should be asked?
choices: the right to have your say
exercises.explain: The right to be listened to (article 12): children should have a say in things that affect them.

exercises.prompt: In 1948 the United Nations wrote a list of rights for whom?
exercises.hint: The children's list came later, in 1989.
exercises.explain: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is for every person; the children's Convention (1989) adds rights just for children.

exercises.prompt: The UN wrote rights for everyone in 1948 and for children in 1989. How many years apart is that?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
matches: a duty you have to others
exercises.hint: Rights are needs; wants are extras.
exercises.explain: A right is what every child needs, a responsibility is a duty to others, and a want is nice to have.

exercises.prompt: Put these in time order, oldest first.
items: you learn about your rights today
exercises.hint: Compare the years: the smaller one came first.
exercises.explain: The rights for every person came in 1948, the children's Convention in 1989, and today you learn about them both.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to the right it is about.
items: a child can't go to school
a child has no time to play
a child is not kept from harm
matches: the right to rest and play
the right to have a say
exercises.hint: Which right is missing in each problem?
exercises.explain: No school breaks the right to learn. Not being asked breaks the right to a say. No time to play breaks the right to rest and play. Not being kept from harm breaks the right to be safe. Grown-ups must protect them all.
